explanation: Represent the virtual array [0,…,n−1] by a map: absent positions contain their own indices. Read both mapped values before swapping positions i and a uniformly chosen suffix position. Return the first k virtual positions.
timeComplexity: O(k) expected: k swaps and k result reads, each using constant expected hash work. Each of k iterations performs a constant number of expected-time hash operations; at most O(k) map entries are introduced.
spaceComplexity: O(k) map entries and O(k) returned values. At most a constant number of virtual-map entries are added per selection, plus k output entries.
attribution: Unmodified reference from epi_judge_python_solutions/random_subset.py; Elements of Programming Interviews Judge contributors; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International, retained in repository LICENSE. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: After step i the map agrees with a real Fisher–Yates shuffle through position i. Reading absent positions as their indices preserves all untouched entries. Each suffix choice is uniform, so the k-prefix is a uniform ordered sample; forgetting its order makes each subset equally likely.
walkthrough: For n=5 and k=2, one possible run chooses virtual position 3, then position 4. It returns [3,4], recording the displaced virtual values only where necessary. Every two-element subset of {0,1,2,3,4} has probability 1/10, regardless of returned order. JSON arguments are [n,k]. Observed true is the property/distribution check, not the callable return.
edgeCases: k=n returns every value in some order.
No selected value can appear twice.
